Recall the following:

* If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ for all $x\in (a,b),$ then $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $(a,b).$

* If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ for all $x\in (a,b),$ then $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $(a,b).$

The graph below shows that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is positive on the interval $(-3,3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202093/assets/c72ad85a6998493f29289074a4750f2830e8fdefe51d6f81536257abfb8ae008.png)

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly increasing when $x\in (-3,3).$

The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on $[-6,6].$ It's known that $f(-3)=-\frac{5\pi }{2}.$ The graph of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ consists of two line segments and a semicircle, as shown above.

feedback.worked_solution:
From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(3)-f(-3) \\ {\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(3)-(-\frac{5\pi }{2}) \\ f(3) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The definite integral of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ over $[-3,3]$ is the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis. The corresponding region is a semicircle, so we find the area using the formula 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x=A=\frac{9\pi }{2}.$ 

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+\frac{9\pi }{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(6)-f(-3) \\ {\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(6)-(-\frac{5\pi }{2}) \\ f(6) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ on $[-3,6]$ consists of two parts: 

* an arc of a quarter circle for $x\in [-3,3],$ which lies above the $x$-axis, and 

* a line segment for $x\in [3,6],$ which lies below the $x$-axis. 

Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}.
$$

The first integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,3].$ Earlier, we found that

$$
{A}_{1}=\frac{9\pi }{2}.
$$

The second integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [3,6].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}ab \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 4 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

However, since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-6.
$$

Therefore, the value of the original integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can find $f(6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(6) & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+{\int }_{-3}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5\pi }{2}+(\frac{9\pi }{2}-6) \\  & =2\pi -6.\end{aligned}
$$
